title: Harnessing vector databases: A comprehensive analysis of their role across industries
relevance_reason: Vector databases are the main subject of the paper; it provides a comprehensive comparative analysis of their core capabilities, advantages, limitations, and industry-specific suitability, making it directly relevant to a survey on vector databases.
research_focus: Comprehensive comparison of leading vector database solutions, analyzing their advantages, limitations, and suitability across industries (finance, healthcare, retail, transportation) based on scalability, query performance, data structure compatibility, and cost-effectiveness.
method: A comparative framework is introduced to evaluate multiple vector database technologies across key factors (scalability, query performance, data structure compatibility, cost-effectiveness), followed by industry-specific application analysis.
application_domain: Cross-industry: recommendation systems, image retrieval, NLP, fraud detection, medical imaging, diagnostic analytics, transaction monitoring, real-time search
results_summary: The paper presents a comprehensive comparison of leading vector database solutions, evaluating them on scalability, query performance, data structure compatibility, and cost-effectiveness. The findings reveal that vector databases offer superior query performance and scalability compared to traditional relational databases. However, integration complexity and cost-effectiveness vary significantly across different solutions. The study provides industry-specific insights for finance, healthcare, retail, and transportation, helping enterprises determine whether adopting a vector database aligns with their operational requirements.
limitations: Integration complexities when adopting vector databases; Cost implications vary across solutions; Scalability concerns persist for some vector database technologies
research_gaps: Refining AI-driven optimization techniques for vector database indexing and query processing; Exploring federated learning to improve privacy-preserving AI applications leveraging vector databases

title: Flexible Similarity Search of Semantic Vectors Using Fulltext Search Engines
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is vector similarity search as core vector database technology: it proposes a specific indexing approach (feature token encoding for inverted indexes) and benchmarks its performance across multiple datasets and similarity measures, making vector search the central topic rather than a tool used for another purpose.
research_focus: Validating a novel method of encoding semantic vectors into feature tokens for inverted-index-based fulltext search engines, and evaluating its performance across diverse datasets (text embeddings and image descriptors) with different similarity measures.
method: Semantic vectors are encoded into 'feature tokens' that are indexed and searched using standard inverted-index-based IR systems (Elasticsearch, Lucene, Sphinx, Solr). The paper evaluates the impact of the number of best features selected and the page size on Precision@10, NDCG@10, and Avg. diff.@10 across multiple datasets with varying dimensionalities and representations.
application_domain: Text document retrieval (NLP/information retrieval) and image search (SIFT descriptors)
results_summary: The paper validates the vector encoding method on datasets including LSA, doc2vec, GloVe text representations and SIFT image descriptors. It shows that keeping only the 90 best features is nearly indistinguishable from using all features in terms of Precision@10, and that dimensionality below 200 significantly degrades retrieval quality. The method achieves an excellent approximation of the gold standard across all tested datasets, confirming its stability and generalizability. Increasing the page size consistently improves relevance at the cost of search performance. The doc2vec dataset showed unusually low Precision@10 due to high mutual similarity among document vectors lacking distinct feature peaks.
limitations: Low-dimensional vectors (≤100 dimensions) cause a significant drop in Precision@10; The doc2vec representation produces vectors with high mutual similarity and lack of distinguishing feature peaks, degrading retrieval precision; Reducing the number of features used for querying decreases the relevance of retrieved documents by all metrics
research_gaps: Tuning doc2vec parameters to better differentiate between documents could solve the low-precision issue observed on that dataset; Further increase in page size would lead to further improvements in relevance at the cost of performance, suggesting a trade-off space not fully explored

title: Comparative Effect of Distance Metrics on Selected Texture Features for Content-Based Image Retrieval System
relevance_reason: The paper is about image retrieval using texture features and comparing distance metrics; the phrase 'feature vector database' refers to a collection of image feature vectors, not vector database technology. No vector database systems, indexing structures, or vector search infrastructure are discussed.
research_focus: The effect of different distance metrics (Euclidean, Manhattan, Cosine, Quadratic-form, Pearson) on the retrieval performance of a Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) system characterized by Tamura and Gabor Wavelet transform texture features.
method: Tamura and Gabor Wavelet transform texture features are extracted from images to build a feature vector database. Five distance metrics are used to match 4 sample query images against image databases of 400 and 600 images (4 classes each). Retrieval performance is evaluated using average precision. The system is implemented in MATLAB.
application_domain: Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) using texture features
results_summary: The paper evaluates five distance metrics for a CBIR system using Tamura and Gabor Wavelet texture features on two image databases (400 and 600 images, 4 classes). For the 400-image database, Manhattan distance gave the best retrieval performance across all feature configurations (Tamura alone, Gabor Wavelet alone, and combined). For the 600-image database, results were mixed: Cosine distance performed best for Tamura features, while Manhattan distance was best for Gabor Wavelet and the combined features. Overall, Manhattan distance was the most consistently top-performing metric. The implementation was done in MATLAB with average precision as the evaluation metric.

title: PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS OF CHROMA, QDRANT, AND FAISS DATABASES
relevance_reason: Vector databases are the main subject of the paper, which directly benchmarks and compares the insertion and query performance of three specific vector database systems (Chroma, Qdrant, Faiss) across multiple dataset sizes.
research_focus: Comparison of insertion and query performance of three open-source vector databases (Chroma, Qdrant, Faiss) on datasets of varying sizes (10,000 to 9,990,000 vectors) from the Deep1B dataset.
method: Vectors from the Deep1B dataset were sequentially inserted into Chroma, Qdrant, and Faiss at ten different sizes. Insertion times (including indexing) and query times (top-10 nearest neighbor search on 1000 randomly selected vectors) were measured on an M1 Max processor with 64 GB RAM. Default similarity metrics were used per database (Squared L2 for Chroma, Cosine for Qdrant, L2 for Faiss). No metadata, replication, or partitioning was applied.
application_domain: General vector similarity search for high-dimensional deep learning embeddings
results_summary: The paper measured insertion and query performance of Chroma, Qdrant, and Faiss across dataset sizes from 10,000 to 9,990,000 vectors. Faiss exhibited the fastest insertion times due to its in-memory operation, while Chroma and Qdrant showed increasing insertion times with growing data volume due to index growth. For queries, Faiss provided optimal performance on small datasets without requiring an index, but its advantage diminished as data size increased due to growing memory requirements. Chroma's disk-based storage and indexing capabilities made it more suitable for larger datasets where memory constraints are a concern. Qdrant in memory showed similar insertion times to its disk-based counterpart, indicating that the in-memory configuration did not significantly improve insertion speed.
limitations: No replication or partitioning was performed on the databases; Vectors were added without metadata, limiting the evaluation to pure vector performance; Only one hardware configuration (M1 Max, 64 GB RAM) was used for all measurements; No swap operation with disk was performed, restricting results to in-memory scenarios for Faiss and Qdrant
research_gaps: Deeper investigation of nuanced performance characteristics across various configurations; Exploration of sharding, partitioning, and replication strategies for optimizing database performance

title: A Comparative Study of Contemporary Learning Paradigms in Bug Report Priority Detection
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily a comparative NLP study on bug report classification; vector databases appear only as a retrieval component within a RAG pipeline and are not analyzed, benchmarked, or discussed in any depth regarding their internal technology.
research_focus: Comparative evaluation of different learning paradigms (BERT-based classifiers, contrastive learning, LLMs, and RAG with vector databases) for automated bug report priority classification across multiple text datasets.
method: Experimental comparative study using bug reports (Mozilla), app reviews, and movie reviews datasets, evaluating transformer encoder classifiers, few-shot LLM inference, and RAG pipelines, with statistical significance testing via student's t-test.
application_domain: NLP / software engineering (automated bug report priority classification)
results_summary: The paper compares BERT-based classifiers, contrastive learning for BERT, few-shot LLM inference, and RAG (using a vector database with SBERT embeddings) for bug report priority classification. Contrastive BERT outperforms other methods in 12 out of 15 cases on the Mozilla dataset, demonstrating that incorporating ordinal class information boosts performance. LLM decoder models without fine-tuning underperform fine-tuned encoder classifiers, especially in domain-specific tasks. RAG improves LLM performance in most cases but is not uniformly helpful, sometimes degrading results for extreme classes. Results vary across domains, with movie reviews yielding the best performance and bug reports the worst due to data quality differences.
limitations: Dataset imbalance causes models to prefer the dominant class (P3), leading to false alarms; RAG is not uniformly helpful and can deteriorate performance for extreme classes (P1, P5); Few-shot demonstrations acquired through random sampling do not suffice for conditioning LLMs to generate correct class labels; Contrastive learning does not yield a consistent advantage over regular fine-tuning in the app reviews domain
research_gaps: Investigate ensemble learning and mixture of experts approaches; Explore fine-tuning LLMs with memory-efficient procedures such as LoRA and QLoRA; Develop alternative representations for software bug reports that exploit code snippets and error logs in a structured way

title: Evaluating RAG System Models Robustness to Hybrid Homoglyph and Emoji-Based Next-Generation Adversarial Prompt Injection
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is adversarial prompt injection and RAG system security; FAISS is mentioned only as the vector database used in the pipeline for index vectorization, with no in-depth discussion of vector database technology, indexing methods, or similarity search.
research_focus: Evaluating the robustness of five RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems against hybrid homoglyph and emoji-based adversarial prompt injection attacks that aim to leak sensitive information from the datastore.
method: A unified Dockerized pipeline was built to run five RAG models, using FAISS as the vector database for index vectorization. Adversarial prompts were generated with templated generators applying various obfuscation types (homoglyph substitution, invisible Unicode, emoji injection, and combinations) against synthetic secrets. Metrics included adversarial leak count, pass vs. block rates, benign leak frequencies, and overall leak rate.
application_domain: LLM security and adversarial robustness of RAG pipelines
results_summary: The paper systematically evaluated five RAG models under obfuscated adversarial prompts and found an average leak rate of approximately 68.3% across all models. Combined obfuscations (e.g., homoglyph plus emoji) were found to be especially effective at amplifying leakage. Models with strong Unicode normalization, such as Llama 3.1, consistently maintained low leakage regardless of obfuscation form, while Phi-3 and DeepSeek R1 7B showed the weakest defenses with leak rates exceeding 60%. The authors conclude that effective RAG defense requires deeper structural handling of input diversity and character encoding beyond surface-level prompt filtering.
limitations: All secrets used are synthetic and may have inherently different semantic effects than true secrets; There may be configuration differences between the Docker Desktop evaluation environment and production deployments
research_gaps: Multi-seed runs for statistical robustness; Larger secret sets for more comprehensive evaluation; Harm evaluation of leaked content; Improved detection methods for obfuscated adversarial prompts; Adaptive defenses against evolving obfuscation techniques

title: Multi-Transformer-Based Ensemble Embedding Model for Enhanced Vector Search in NoSQL Database: A Comparative Statistical and Performance Analysis
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is the comparison and ensembling of transformer-based embedding models for semantic search quality, with MongoDB used merely as a storage tool. Vector databases are not the focus of analysis, comparison, or improvement; the contribution lies in embedding model selection and ensemble strategy.
research_focus: Comparative evaluation of three transformer-based embedding models (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2, all-distilroberta-v1) and their ensemble with PCA for enhanced semantic vector search on Wikipedia documents stored in MongoDB, assessed using TREC questions.
method: 2,000 Wikipedia JSON documents are converted into vectors using three transformer-based embedding models, ensembled together, and PCA is applied for dimensionality reduction before storage in MongoDB. Performance is evaluated on 996 TREC questions using metrics including Precision@10, Recall, MRR, F1 score, average execution time, and memory usage.
indexing_methods: PCA; cosine similarity; Euclidean distance; k-nearest neighbor search; product quantisation; inverted file; graph-based ANN indexes
application_domain: Semantic text search and information retrieval on Wikipedia documents
results_summary: The paper compared three transformer-based embedding models individually and as an ensemble with PCA for vector search on 2,000 Wikipedia documents evaluated with 996 TREC questions. The ensemble+PCA approach achieved the highest average F1 score of 0.5094, with improved precision@10 and recall over individual models. However, the ensemble process increased memory usage to 924.79 MB and average query execution time to 0.1031 seconds. The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model had narrow embedding values close to zero, limiting retrieval effectiveness, while all-distilroberta-v1 had lower query execution time but failed to achieve a high F1 score. The authors concluded that the ensemble+PCA method is suitable for large-scale dataset processing and real-time applications.
limitations: The ensemble process abruptly increased memory usage to 924.79 MB, higher than individual models; Average execution time for each query increased to 0.1031 seconds with the ensemble; all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding values are narrow to zero, failing to retrieve information effectively; all-distilroberta-v1 failed to retrieve information effectively compared to other models despite lower query execution time; Higher dimensionality of vector data increases query execution time and creates complexity in finding similarity with large databases
research_gaps: Limited explorations on MiniLM-based models for text-to-vector transformation and query retrieval using MongoDB; Computational efficiency and information retrieval from different queries are not examined statistically in prior work; Custom rule-based advanced filtering methods are needed to reduce complexity in MiniLM models; Transforming long texts into clauses could improve similarity search for the paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2 model; The all-distilroberta-v1 model should be evaluated specifically for complex queries rather than general queries

title: Using Vector Databases for the Selection of Related Occupations: An Empirical Evaluation Using O*NET
relevance_reason: The paper examines vector databases in real depth by comparing two systems (Milvus and Chroma), analyzing the impact of multiple configuration parameters (distance metrics, embeddings, text composition), and reporting detailed retrieval measurements, but the main subject is the application to occupation retrieval rather than vector database technology itself.
research_focus: Systematic empirical evaluation of two open-source vector databases (Milvus and Chroma) for retrieving related occupations from the O*NET database, analyzing the impact of document structure, sentence embeddings, and distance metrics on retrieval quality compared to curated explicit relations.
method: Experimental evaluation using two vector databases with multiple configurations (different distance metrics, sentence embedding models including JobBERT, CareerBERT, and all_mpnet_base_v2, and different text fragment compositions), benchmarked against curated related-occupation relations in O*NET, with statistical analysis via Kruskal-Wallis H-test and mutual information estimation.
mentioned_systems: Milvus; Chroma; O*NET; ESCO; JobBERT; CareerBERT; all_mpnet_base_v2; gbert-base; scikit-learn
application_domain: Career planning, occupation retrieval, job search and transition
results_summary: The paper evaluated Milvus and Chroma across multiple configurations for retrieving related occupations from O*NET, finding that distance metrics, sentence embeddings, and text fragment selection are all statistically significant for retrieval performance. Precision is high (above 0.8) for smaller result cutoffs (k < 5), which is particularly relevant for RAG and few-shot prompting settings. The two databases showed very small differences in overall results, indicating that configuration elements rather than database implementation are the primary determinants of retrieval quality. Text-based retrieval only partially overlaps with curated explicit relations but also discovers cross-cutting relations not captured in the hierarchical database structure, suggesting that text retrieval should complement rather than replace curated relations in practical applications.
limitations: Does not consider any concrete context-specific task (e.g., career shift vs. career growth in the same domain) that would affect which text elements are most relevant for retrieval; Difficult to assess the extent to which content limitations of the O*NET database itself (sparse coverage in some areas, redundancy in others) affect retrieval metrics; No alternative occupational databases were found that could be used to mitigate the O*NET content limitations
research_gaps: Assess the combination of vector database retrieval with LLMs in RAG or GraphRAG patterns, accounting for the separate contribution of the retrieval part and the LLM; Further experimentation with other occupational databases such as ESCO that have different database schemas, contents, scope, and coverage; Expert assessment of discovered relations (retrieved occupations not in the curated set) to evaluate their validity and usefulness

title: A Experimental Analysis of Vector Databases for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Pipelines: Performance, Scalability, and Use-Case Suitability Submission Details
relevance_reason: Vector databases are the main subject of the paper, which proposes a comprehensive comparative benchmark of six systems across core performance metrics (latency, recall, throughput) and provides a decision framework for selecting among them.
research_focus: A comprehensive comparative benchmark of six leading vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, pgvector, ChromaDB) evaluated across query latency, recall accuracy, throughput scalability, cost efficiency, and RAG pipeline suitability.
method: Evaluation using public benchmarks (ANN-Benchmarks, BEIR, MTEB) with 1,536-dimensional embeddings, measuring multiple performance metrics, and applying a weighted decision framework to produce composite scores and use-case recommendations.
mentioned_systems: Pinecone; Qdrant; Weaviate; Milvus; pgvector; ChromaDB
application_domain: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines and production AI application patterns
results_summary: The paper benchmarked six vector databases using public benchmarks with 1,536-dimensional embeddings across latency, recall, throughput, cost, and RAG suitability. Qdrant achieved the lowest P99 latency (9.8 ms) and highest throughput (5,900 QPS at 10M vectors). A weighted decision framework assigned Qdrant the highest composite score (9.06/10). Practical recommendations were provided for seven production AI application patterns, including starting with Qdrant for new projects, migrating to Milvus beyond 100M vectors, and using pgvector when PostgreSQL is already in the stack. The paper addresses three identified gaps in prior comparative studies by evaluating current versions, using holistic metrics, and including RAG-integrated end-to-end evaluation.
limitations: Benchmark results reflect specific hardware configurations and may not generalise across all deployment environments; Managed service evaluations (Pinecone, Weaviate Cloud) are subject to network latency variability absent in self-hosted comparisons; The rapidly evolving nature of the field means performance characteristics may shift substantially with new software releases; Multi-modal vector databases were not evaluated due to scope constraints
research_gaps: Prior comparative studies evaluate legacy versions predating major 2024-2025 performance updates; Prior studies focus on single metrics rather than holistic production readiness; Prior studies lack RAG-integrated end-to-end evaluation

title: A unified benchmarking framework for vector databases in scalable embedding-based image retrieval systems
relevance_reason: Vector databases are the main subject of the paper: it proposes a unified benchmarking framework, performs a detailed cross-system comparison of four vector databases across the full data lifecycle, analyzes their indexing architectures (HNSW, IVF, PQ), and provides deployment recommendations specifically for vector database selection.
research_focus: Development of a unified benchmarking framework that evaluates four vector databases (FAISS, Milvus, Qdrant, pgvector) across the full data lifecycle (setup, insertion, querying, update, deletion, accuracy) using real image embeddings, combined with a workload-aware multi-criteria scoring model for deployment recommendations.
method: A reproducible benchmarking pipeline on a single consumer workstation (8 GB RAM) using dual-model embeddings (CLIP ViT-B/32 and ResNet-50) on CIFAR-10 and STL-10 datasets at scales from 100 to 50,000 vectors. Metrics include setup time, insertion throughput, query latency (Top-K, filtered, range), update/delete cost, recall, precision, mAP, and memory usage. A multi-objective scoring scheme connected to AHP and Pareto efficiency analysis translates raw metrics into deployment recommendations. Architectural root-cause analysis links empirical measurements to internal design choices.
mentioned_systems: FAISS; Milvus; Qdrant; pgvector; Weaviate; Pinecone; Chroma
application_domain: Embedding-based image retrieval (visual search, recommendation systems, medical image retrieval, retrieval-augmented generation)
results_summary: Controlled experiments on CIFAR-10 and STL-10 across scales from 100 to 50,000 vectors confirm that no single vector database dominates across all performance dimensions, and relative rankings are consistent across different embedding distributions. FAISS delivers exceptional raw speed via in-memory SIMD-accelerated architecture but lacks persistence and native metadata filtering. Milvus provides the most balanced performance among persistent systems, combining perfect recall with stable latency through IVF cluster partitioning. Qdrant excels in update flexibility and filtered queries but suffers recall degradation (0.82 on STL-10, 0.88 on CIFAR-10) due to greedy HNSW traversal failing in dense embedding neighborhoods, mitigable by raising the ef parameter. pgvector integrates seamlessly with PostgreSQL but incurs a fundamental insertion penalty from the conflict between WAL sequential-flush optimization and HNSW random graph edge construction.
limitations: Limited to 50,000 vectors due to 8 GB system RAM constraint, preventing stress testing of FAISS near-RAM-capacity behavior; Single-node deployments only; no distributed multi-node evaluation of Milvus or Qdrant; Consumer-grade hardware only; no server-class or GPU-accelerated benchmarking; No million-scale evaluation (SIFT1M, Deep1M) performed; Scoring model relies on user-set priorities rather than academically validated weight elicitation (AHP applied conceptually, not experimentally)
research_gaps: Server-class hardware validation and million-scale dataset evaluation on SIFT1M and Deep1M; Distributed multi-node evaluation of Milvus and Qdrant to characterize horizontal scalability; GPU-accelerated FAISS benchmarking; AHP-based weight elicitation for the scoring model; Concurrent workload benchmarking; Systematic parameter tuning sweeps; Extended embedding model coverage (DINOv2, SigLIP); Full cloud-deployed total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis; Evaluation of additional databases including Weaviate, Pinecone, and Chroma

title: Federated Retrieval Over Heterogeneous Vector Stores: An Empirical Characterization with ImperaBench-CART
relevance_reason: The paper substantially discusses vector databases—federation across multiple stores, their incompatible score spaces, per-source latency, and the design of a federated retrieval client—but its main subject is the federation problem and the benchmark methodology for chunk-retrieval, not vector database core technology (indexing, ANN search algorithms) itself.
research_focus: The federation problem when multiple vector databases with different embedding models are used together: specifically, why score-magnitude-based merging of per-source ranked outputs fails to identify the answer-holding source, and the actual recall difficulty of chunk-retrieval measured against independent ground truth.
method: Empirical characterization using ImperaBench-CART, a chunk-anchored benchmark of 354 queries over 5,933 chunks from 20 open-access biomedical papers, evaluating nine retrieval configurations (three native single-store, three heterogeneous federated, three homogeneous federated) with 95% bootstrap CIs and pairwise McNemar tests, plus latency/throughput measurements under load.
application_domain: Biomedical retrieval (CAR-T therapy in B-cell lymphoma) and enterprise RAG systems spanning multiple vector stores
results_summary: The paper demonstrates that score-magnitude-based merging cannot reliably identify the answer-holding source, with the correct source's top-1 score being highest in only 34.5% of queries under heterogeneous embedders—statistically indistinguishable from the three-source chance rate. Federation matches the per-embedder recall ceiling (recall@10 of 20–30%, recall@1 of 5–9%) without degrading retrieval, but pays a ~1.7× p50 latency cost and ~4.5× throughput cost under load attributable to the slowest participating embedder. The Tier-0 vs Tier-1 paraphrase gap of +0 to +9 percentage points is shown to be a property of dense retrievers rather than federation. The paper further shows that prior chunk-retrieval evaluations using self-referential (embedder-defined) ground truth inflate recall by approximately 25×, and releases the Impera library with a per-source contract that defers cross-source ranking to the application via five pluggable merge strategies.
limitations: Single-domain corpus: all papers concern CAR-T therapy in B-cell lymphoma, limiting quantitative generalization to other biomedical subfields or domains; Sample size of 354 queries is sufficient for tight CIs at the observed recall range but requires paired McNemar tests for small improvements; LLM-drafted queries (Sonnet 4.6 for Tier-0, Haiku 4.5 for Tier-1) inherit question-style biases from those models; Single test split: the benchmark is evaluation-only; reranker training or embedder fine-tuning requires a paper-disjoint holdout to avoid contamination; The 0.25 Jaccard equivalence threshold was selected empirically and different thresholds produce different qrels; No lexical baseline: only dense retrievers are evaluated; BM25 and hybrid dense+lexical baselines are left to future work
research_gaps: Better domain-adapted embedders for the corpus; Query expansion or decomposition before retrieval; Multi-stage pipelines that trade latency for recall; BM25 and hybrid dense+lexical baselines on the same qrels; Reducing the Tier-0 vs Tier-1 paraphrase gap via embedder fine-tuning on paraphrase pairs

title: VecBench: A Controllable Benchmark for Filtered Vector Search: [Experiments & Analysis]
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate filtered vector search in vector databases, including data generation, query synthesis, and unified performance metrics for vector database systems. It directly contributes to the core technology of vector databases (indexing, similarity search, and system evaluation).
research_focus: Proposing VecBench, a controllable benchmark for holistic evaluation of filtered vector search in vector databases, addressing limitations of existing benchmarks in data realism, workload design, and dynamic evaluation.
method: VecBench combines three components: (1) controllable vector data generation using random linear projection based on the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma with a provable error bound, (2) distribution-aware query synthesis with adjustable selectivity and filter correlation supporting multi-type predicates, and (3) a unified evaluation metric covering six phases including concurrent query processing and dynamic update scenarios. Extensive experiments are conducted on ten representative filtered search approaches across four vector databases.
mentioned_systems: Pgvector; Milvus; Qdrant; Big-ANN; VectorDBBench; BigVectorBench
application_domain: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for large language models, e-commerce product image search, and document search with structured attribute filters
results_summary: The paper proposes VecBench to overcome three limitations of existing filtered vector search benchmarks: low-dimensional datasets, simplistic random filter workloads, and lack of dynamic evaluation. VecBench enables controllable data generation with provable error bounds, fine-grained workload control over selectivity and filter correlation, and a unified six-phase evaluation framework. Experiments on ten approaches across four vector databases demonstrate that increasing dimensionality and scale by 10x causes substantial latency increases (e.g., 15x for Pgvector), and that different databases achieve best recall under different filter correlation settings (e.g., Milvus best at correlation=0, Pgvector best at correlation=0.5). The results validate VecBench as a tool for systematically stress-testing diverse filtered search strategies under both static and dynamic scenarios.

title: BigVectorBench: Heterogeneous Data Embedding and Compound Queries are Essential in Evaluating Vector Databases
relevance_reason: Vector databases are the main subject of the paper: it proposes a new benchmark (BigVectorBench) specifically designed to evaluate vector database performance, conducts extensive experiments on Milvus, Weaviate, and Qdrant, and identifies performance bottlenecks in their core operations (embedding, indexing, and compound query handling).
research_focus: The paper addresses the gap in existing vector database benchmarks that overlook heterogeneous data embedding and compound queries, proposing BigVectorBench as an integrated benchmark framework to evaluate both embedding performance and compound query handling in vector databases.
method: The authors designed and developed BigVectorBench, an extensible benchmark framework comprising five datasets, ten workloads, and four fundamental compound query types, and conducted hundreds of experiments on Milvus, Weaviate, and Qdrant to evaluate embedding latency, retrieval throughput, and recall under various conditions.
indexing_methods: HNSW; IVFPQ; tree-based indexes; hash-based indexes; quantization indexes; graph-based indexes; inverted indexing
application_domain: Vector database benchmarking and evaluation, with applications in RAG for LLMs, recommendation systems, and bioinformatics
results_summary: The evaluation reveals that embedding latency, not similarity search latency, is the primary bottleneck in serving user queries, often exceeding hundreds of milliseconds in multimodal scenarios. Compound queries significantly reduce both QPS and recall, with recall nearly halving compared to unimodal queries. Milvus's HNSW index shows a QPS decline of over 53% when the filter ratio falls below 7%, as it transitions from approximate to exact search. Milvus's IVFPQ algorithm exhibits recall below 40% at 1536 and 3072 dimensions due to limitations of clustered algorithms in high-dimensional spaces. Unified embedding models struggle to align audio and text, resulting in compound query recall rates below 0.4% across all three databases.
limitations: Current vector database optimizations focus mainly on improving indexing for faster retrieval, neglecting embedding performance enhancements; Unified embedding models face challenges in accurately aligning audio and text data; Clustered algorithms such as IVFPQ encounter difficulties distinguishing closely positioned data points in high-dimensional spaces
research_gaps: A critical need for a unified embedding model to align multimodal data and decrease embedding latency effectively; An evident demand for advanced indexing mechanisms that enhance the handling of compound queries; Existing benchmarks overlook heterogeneous data embedding and compound queries, creating a gap in evaluating vector database performance
